purpose: Connect the recorded model behavior to internationally recognized indicators and documented recruitment, financing and collection mechanisms.
relationship_to_benchmarks: This expanded interpretive crosswalk was assembled after the frozen runs. Some source summaries overlap earlier packets. Original prompts, supplied evidence, reference labels, observations and recorded grades remain unchanged; no model is represented as having been tested on this complete new packet.

sources.title: Protocol to Prevent, Suppress and Punish Trafficking in Persons, Especially Women and Children, supplementing the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime
sources.location: A/RES/55/25, Annex II, Article 3(a)-(d), printed pp. 32-33; PDF indices 31-32.
sources.summary: The adult definition combines a specified act, a listed means and an exploitation purpose. Consent to intended exploitation is irrelevant where a listed means is used. For children, the means element is unnecessary; child means under 18.
sources.scope: Treaty definition and criminalization framework. Assess each element and supporting facts separately; individual liability and territorial application require their own analysis. Article 3 contains no border-crossing element.

sources.title: ILO indicators of forced labour: 2025 revised edition
sources.location: Sections 1.1 and 2.2, printed pp. 3, 5-6; sections 3.6-3.9, pp. 16-23 (PDF indices 8-11).
sources.summary: Explains threats, document retention, wage withholding and debt bondage through coercion and constrained consent. It includes forced return of wages after bank payment and deliberate debt manipulation.
sources.scope: Frontline detection and referral guidance. Interpret combinations and the worker's circumstances; one indicator alone does not confirm forced labour. Protective inquiry and a categorical finding are distinct.

sources.title: General principles and operational guidelines for fair recruitment and definition of recruitment fees and related costs
sources.location: General principle 7; definition of recruitment fees and related costs; publication description.
sources.summary: The fair-recruitment benchmark allocates recruitment fees and related costs away from workers, including indirect charging. The definition covers the substance of the cost rather than its label.
sources.scope: Tripartite principles and operational guidance. Distinguish this benchmark, applicable treaty obligations and jurisdiction-specific offences; a fee concern alone supplies neither every trafficking element nor a universal domestic-law conclusion.

sources.title: Indebted Before Departure: Information Arbitrage and Financial Exploitation by Philippine Migration Intermediaries
sources.date: Publication day unstated; fieldwork 2021-05-05 to 2021-05-16; publisher-hosted edition in 2022
sources.location: Methods pp. 12-13; compulsory-provider/referral analysis pp. 20-28; money-provider Figures 4.b/5.b, p. 25.
sources.summary: Migrasia's 961-person OFW survey documents agency pressure and referrals to selected training centres, clinics and money providers, alongside migration-related debt.
sources.scope: Pollfish mobile-app sampling with gender quotas and geographic exclusions; digital and age/location biases acknowledged. Self-reported relationships support inquiry, rather than proof of corporate collusion or a criminal finding.

sources.title: Exploited for Profit, Failed by Governments: Indonesian Migrant Domestic Workers Trafficked to Hong Kong
sources.location: Index ASA 17/029/2013; methods pp. 15-16; section 9.2, pp. 63-65; document retention section 9.6, pp. 70-71.
sources.summary: Documents agency-linked finance-company loans, diverted salaries, third-party repayments, collection pressure involving families or employers and false full-wage receipts.
sources.scope: 97 non-random interviews with Indonesian domestic workers who experienced migration problems, plus a separately sourced 930-person IMWU survey. Historical evidence of mechanisms; not a current population estimate or a finding about every lender.

sources.title: Coming Clean: The prevalence of forced labour and human trafficking for the purpose of forced labour amongst migrant domestic workers in Hong Kong
sources.location: Methods and limits pp. 32-39; recruitment debt pp. 44-45; freedom to quit p. 51; subgroup associations p. 55.
sources.summary: Examines recruitment debt, practical freedom to quit and forced-labour indicators among 1,003 currently employed migrant domestic workers, with 46 focus-group participants.
sources.scope: April-May 2015 survey: 11 geographic clusters, systematic interception and nationality quotas. Local adaptation of an ILO measurement framework; associations are not individual adjudications or causal proof.
sources.access_note: Indexed primary-PDF text was inspected. The publisher's base URL currently redirects to its successor site, ASK; preserve the original bibliographic citation when locating an archived copy.

sources.title: Overview of International Migrant Workers in the Care, Hospitality, and Entertainment and Informal Economy Sectors in Hong Kong SAR, China
sources.location: Methods pp. 5-7; recruitment costs and financing pp. 23-26; employment-related risks from p. 27.
sources.summary: Produced by Migrasia and the University of Hong Kong under IOM's CREST initiative. Connects recruitment financing and salary deductions with employment vulnerability and reports risks involving training, medical and lending intermediaries.
sources.scope: 150-worker survey, 18 worker interviews, 11 employer interviews and 16 key informants. Purposive/place-based and respondent-driven recruitment; 40-60% reported refusal rates. The authors explicitly limit statistical generalization.

sources.title: The Role of Recruitment Fees and Abusive and Fraudulent Recruitment Practices of Recruitment Agencies in Trafficking in Persons
sources.location: Section 1.2, methods pp. 2-4; recruitment-fee and debt discussion pp. 8-12; coercive-recruitment indicators p. 16.
sources.summary: Explains how recruitment fees, borrowing, deception and coercive recruitment can connect to trafficking, including debts and financial commitments that constrain workers' choices.
sources.scope: Literature/case-law review, expert meetings and 47 expert consultations in Indonesia, Peru, Bahrain and the UAE. A comparative mechanisms study, rather than a representative worker-prevalence survey.

sources.title: Financial Flows from Human Trafficking
sources.location: Paragraph 10, p. 6; methodology pp. 7-8; forced-labour typologies pp. 26-29 (PDF indices 27-30).
sources.summary: Describes manipulated debt, identity-document retention, immigration threats and third-party control of wages or bank accounts. Financial analysis follows actors, beneficiaries and actual flows rather than relying on business labels.
sources.scope: FATF-APG literature review, contributed cases, workshops and financial-sector/NGO input. Typologies and financial red flags guide investigation; they are not prevalence estimates or proof that an unexplained payment is trafficking.

indicators.indicator: Debt bondage or manipulated recruitment debt
indicators.evidence_question: Does repayment pressure compel continued work or prevent exit, and are the debt terms, balance or deductions manipulated?
Can the worker retrieve and use original documents freely, or is access conditioned on payment, permission or continued work?

indicators.indicator: Withheld wages or controlled wage access
indicators.evidence_question: Who controls earned pay in practice, including any compelled return or transfer after the salary reaches an account?

indicators.kind: ILO threat indicator plus documented collection mechanism
indicators.evidence_question: What threats target the worker, family, job or immigration position, and how do they affect refusal, disclosure and leaving?

indicators.indicator: Compulsory referrals to lenders, clinics or training providers
indicators.evidence_question: Can the worker choose another provider without losing the job, deployment, documents or money? Who requires the referral and benefits?
Who arranges financing, receives payments and directs collection, and what evidence connects those roles beyond shared names or addresses?

indicators.indicator: Deceptive terms or misleading payment records
indicators.kind: ILO deception indicator plus documented financial mechanism
indicators.evidence_question: Do promised terms, receipts, actual receipts of money and ultimate payment recipients agree, and does any mismatch constrain the worker?

indicators.indicator: Worker-borne recruitment fees and related costs
indicators.evidence_question: Who ultimately bears each recruitment cost, including indirect charges or a renamed reimbursement, and which standard or legal rule is being assessed?

indicators.indicator: Palermo act, means and exploitation purpose
indicators.evidence_question: Which act, listed means and exploitation purpose are supported for an adult, which remain unknown, and does the child-specific rule apply?

recommended_assessment_layers: Record supported facts, missing facts and source spans before assigning an indicator judgment.
Assess international indicator/standard compatibility separately from individual domestic criminal certainty.
Rank concrete protective actions by immediate risk, worker choice, confidentiality and safe conditions; retain several appropriate actions or a specified information gap where needed.
Compare an actual benign worker-control condition and optional ordinary assistance, rather than forcing every case into an intervention.
Use a new version for any source-informed re-evaluation. Preserve the original source prompts, inputs, reference definitions and observations.
execution_boundary: The prepared Jev menu/ILO study has 72 requested, 1 attempted HTTP 402 outcome, 0 usable observations and 71 unattempted. This crosswalk supplies no new Jev result or model-performance estimate.
privacy: Source mechanisms and aggregate methods only; no survivor quotations or identifiable personal case details.
